item.title: M-Red-Team: AsyncAPI Supply Chain Compromise via GitHub Actions
item.description:
M-Red-Team supply chain attack hit AsyncAPI via a GitHub Actions "pwn request," stealing a privileged PAT and publishing five malicious npm package versions reaching 3M+ downloads per week.
Key details:
- The attacker exploited a pull_request_target misconfiguration in asyncapi/generator: the workflow ran in the base repo context with secret access, but checked out attacker-controlled PR code. PR hid obfuscated JavaScript after ~1,000 bytes of whitespace; the workflow exfiltrated secrets to rentry[.]co/elzotebo at 05:16 UTC, 8 minutes after the PR opened. A fix had been proposed and sat unmerged for 58 days.
- Five malicious versions across four packages were published under @asyncapi: generator 3.3.1, generator-helpers 1.1.1, generator-components 0.7.1, and specs 6.11.2 and 6.11.2-alpha.1. Payload executes on import/require, not install, bypassing install-time scanning.
- The three-stage chain: Stage 1 spawns a detached process on import; Stage 2 downloads an 8.25 MB encrypted bundle from IPFS; Stage 3 is a 92,000-line framework (self-labeled "M-RED-TEAM v6.4") persisting via a systemd user service (miasma-monitor.service) and using HTTP, Nostr relays, Ethereum smart contracts, and libp2p for C2.
- Credential theft targets browser passwords and cookies, SSH keys, npm and GitHub tokens, AWS credentials, macOS Keychain, and crypto wallets across developer and CI/CD environments.

item.title: The Jalisco Toolkit and AI-Powered Phishing Surge
item.description:
Two newly identified MFA-bypass toolkits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, are hitting Microsoft 365 environments in 2026 alongside AI-powered PhaaS kits driving a 1,380% phishing surge. Device code phishing is displacing credential theft as the dominant technique.
- Jalisco is a device code phishing toolkit that uses lure-generation: rather than baking a static OAuth code into the page, it calls a backend API to provision a fresh code per session in real time, defeating the 15-minute TTL that defenders rely on. The attacker never touches the victim's password. OAuth access and refresh tokens are silently harvested from Microsoft's token endpoint, meaning password resets and credential monitoring provide zero relief. Confirmed IOCs include authplanned[.]online, grantfundingapplications[.]com, sessionopen0[.]site, and levaquin2us[.]top.
- Post-compromise persistence goes through Entra ID device enrollment. Attackers are enrolling 5+ attacker-controlled devices per compromised account using names like "microsoft-*" and "WINDOWS-*" to blend in. Each enrolled device holds a Primary Refresh Token that auto-renews, surviving password resets and session revocations. Exfiltration from SharePoint and SaaS platforms has been observed in as little as six minutes.
- OmegaLord is a JavaScript credential harvester that impersonates a PDF reader and explicitly collects phone numbers alongside passwords, a deliberate step toward intercepting SMS-based MFA.

item.title: SeasonalInvite: New Phishing Campaign Abuses eCards and RMM
item.description:
SeasonalInvite: 959-domain phishing campaign active since January 2026 abuses legitimate RMM tools across Windows and macOS via fake eCard lures, AI-generated landing pages, and a shared traffic distribution system.
- Six months of seasonal pivots (tax, Valentine's, Easter, spring RSVPs) funnel victims to BlueMountain-impersonating pages that auto-download OS-specific payloads after 3 seconds. The fingerprint string "Your exclusive eCard will download automatically in 3 seconds" appears verbatim on all 959 domains. Windows variants drop ScreenConnect, LogMeIn Resolve, or O&O Syspectr via BAT, VBS, or MSI; macOS gets a legitimate unmodified Kaseya PKG paired with a config.data sidecar that redirects enrollment to attacker infrastructure, bypassing Gatekeeper entirely.
- Anti-forensics are baked in: VBS droppers use ping 127.0.0.1 -n 4 as a delay before self-deleting, MSIs are written to C:\Windows\Temp or C:\Temp as adobeeinstaller.msi or SC_Setup.msi, and curl.exe runs with --ssl-no-revoke. ScreenConnect sessions are tagged with campaign labels like RsvpInvitation for operator tracking.
- Key defanged IOCs from the report: payload server 64.34.84[.]93, C2 westseattlehc.screenconnect[.]com, staging host pub-80959acc7e1349d797b303af25aad569.r2[.]dev, dropper domain drleic[.]top, TDS gate lanero[.]vu. Infrastructure overlaps with a LogoKit credential harvester on 46.4.120[.]162.

item.title: ​​Kratos PhaaS Targets US and EU: How to Reduce Microsoft 365 Account Takeover Risk​
item.description:
Kratos PhaaS is a maturing Microsoft 365 credential-theft platform active since Sept 2025, with 1,484 previously unattributed sandbox sessions now linked to the family across 20+ countries.
- Kratos runs three page generations (V0, V1, V2), each with distinct exfiltration endpoints: V0 POSTs to /PTT/SOft/mini.php, V1 to next.php/nex.php/n3xt.php, V2 to save.php. The kit chains legitimate platforms (SharePoint, Canva, DocuSign lures) through Cloudflare Turnstile anti-bot checks before serving a fake Microsoft 365 login. Browser tab title is nearly always "Authentication" and an animated envelope with "Loading in progress..." precedes the credential form.
- The single best hunting fingerprint: HTTP requests to both /assets/img/barr.svg and /assets/img/lg.svg in the same session. That pair yields 90% recall with near-zero false positives. Key hashes: lg.svg = cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea, styles.css = c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb (connects 636 tasks across V1 and V2).

item.title: The serpent’s tongue: Luring the Python out of its den
item.description:
Python supply chain attacks execute payloads at install time, not runtime. Cisco Talos maps every abuse technique across the package lifecycle, from setup.py hooks to .pth persistence, giving defenders a structured hunt framework.
- Build hook abuses are the highest-risk vector. A malicious setup.py runs arbitrary code the moment pip install fires, before the developer ever imports a line. Worse, .pth files dropped into site-packages or dist-packages execute on every Python invocation persistently, a technique TeamPCP used in the litellm supply chain compromise. The VIPERTUNNEL backdoor abused sitecustomize.py the same way.
- Attackers also manipulate PYTHONPATH via setup.py to redirect module resolution at the user-profile level, surviving new shell sessions silently.
- Package content abuses cover __init__.py payload hiding (fires on import), __main__.py abuse (fires on python -m), entry point hijacking to shadow legitimate binaries like netstat, and package directory collisions to overwrite functions inside trusted libraries such as pandas.read_json without touching the original distribution name.
- Dwell time context matters here: payload execution can begin within minutes of install, exfiltration within an hour, and credential operationalization by other actors within days. Average dwell time once compromised was nine days per the article.

item.title: CrashStealer: New macOS Infostealer Uses Signed Apps to Evade Gatekeeper
item.description:
CrashStealer is a native C++ macOS infostealer using a signed, notarized dropper to clear Gatekeeper, then stealing credentials, keychains, and ~80 crypto wallet extensions before AES-256-GCM encrypting everything on-device.
- Initial access arrives via "Werkbit Setup.dmg" containing Werkbit.app, signed under Developer ID Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV) and notarized, clearing Gatekeeper silently. The dropper queries the GitHub API at mgothiclove/pkeys for sys.cache, which returns a curl command pulling a Base64-encoded shell script from endpoint-api-v1[.]com, decoded at runtime and piped directly to bash, never touching disk in readable form.
- The script drops CrashReporter.dmg to /tmp, mounts it with hdiutil -nobrowse -noverify, copies the payload to /tmp/.CrashReporter, strips and re-signs it ad-hoc, then launches it. An app bundle executing from a hidden path under /private/tmp is a high-confidence behavioral indicator.
- Collection targets Chrome, Brave, Edge, Firefox, ~80 crypto wallet extensions (MetaMask, Phantom, Coinbase), 14 password managers (1Password, Bitwarden, LastPass), and the login keychain, unlocked using the victim's validated password via dscl -authonly. Encrypted archives with .zx_ prefix land in ~/.cache/com.apple.crashreporter/ and survive staging cleanup, making them a reliable artifact.
- Persistence via LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.crashreporter.helper.plist with KeepAlive/SuccessfulExit false.

item.title: NSA, CISA and allies urge router hardening across critical infrastructure against FSB Center 16 attacks
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 FSB Center 16 (Berserk Bear/Dragonfly) is actively exploiting misconfigured routers across US 🇺🇸 critical infrastructure. NSA, CISA, and allied agencies issued joint guidance after sustained targeting of energy, defense, healthcare, and government sectors.
- FSB Center 16 scans internet-facing IP ranges for SNMP agents accepting default community strings, then sends SNMP Set-Requests from spoofed IPs with OIDs that force devices to export configs, typically saved as config.bkp or output.txt, then exfiltrated via TFTP to actor-controlled VPS or compromised FTP servers. Those config files expose network topology, credentials, ACLs, VPN settings, and trusted connections.
- Known CVEs exploited include CVE-2018-0171 and CVE-2008-41281 targeting Cisco devices, alongside abuse of Cisco Smart Install (SMI) and web management portals. Many TTPs overlap with Salt Typhoon activity.
- Network devices sit outside standard EDR coverage, making SNMP config exports and unauthorized account creation nearly invisible without dedicated network telemetry.
Takeaway: Immediately inventory internet-facing routers. Disable Cisco Smart Install and SNMPv1/v2. Deploy SNMPv3 with auth and encryption. Remove default community strings (public, private). Block TFTP and SMI at perimeter firewalls. Hunt for unexpected files named config.bkp or output.txt on FTP servers and review SNMP logs for Set-Request activity to external IPs. Full mitigations in the joint advisory.

item.title: WhatsApp forensics in 2026 and what survives end-to-end encryption
item.description:
WhatsApp forensics in 2026: E2E encryption protects the wire, not the device. Spyrtacus and the Cellebrite-Pivovarov case both confirm the endpoint is the target, and the artifacts are richer than most examiners expect.
- Android splits evidence across /data/data/com.whatsapp/databases/msgstore.db (live, unencrypted chats), wa.db (contacts), and /sdcard/WhatsApp/Databases/msgstore.db.crypt15 (daily encrypted backup). The 64-byte key at /data/data/com.whatsapp/files/key is required to decrypt; crypt15 uses a protobuf-encoded key with rotating parameters that broke older single-format scripts. wa-crypt-tools by ElDavoo handles the full crypt15 pipeline and remains the most maintained open-source option.
- iOS consolidates messages, group metadata, and media references in /private/var/mobile/Containers/Shared/AppGroup/GUID/ChatStorage.sqlite under the ZWAMESSAGE table. Critical detail: ZMESSAGEDATE uses Core Data epoch (seconds since 2001-01-01), not Unix time. Merging Android and iOS timelines without correcting this produces timestamp drift that can look like tampering.
- The Spyrtacus campaign (fake WhatsApp APK delivered via social engineering to ~200 Italian 🇮🇹 users) left no trace in msgstore.db. The evidence lived in SMS history, browser history, package installation timestamps, installer source, and accessibility service grants. A WhatsApp exam that stops at the chat database is an incomplete exam.

item.title: Defending SaaS-based applications against ShinyHunters OAuth abuse
item.description:
ShinyHunters abused OAuth trust relationships across Salesforce tenants via vishing, SaaS supply chain compromise, and misconfigured guest access, enabling quiet, large-scale CRM exfiltration from mid-2025 through mid-2026.
- Three intrusion paths, all exploiting inherited trust: vishing campaigns impersonated IT support to socially engineer victims into granting OAuth consent to a fake Salesforce Data Loader app (T1566.004, T1528); supply chain attacks compromised Salesloft Drift credentials in August 2025 and Gainsight integrations in November 2025 to harvest OAuth tokens reused across multiple customer tenants; and a guest-access path abused misconfigured Salesforce Aura endpoints using chained GraphQL queries to bypass record-retrieval limits and bulk-extract CRM data without authenticating.
- The June 2026 Klue incident tied to Storm-3138 adds a named actor overlap. IOCs from that campaign: 138.226.246[.]94, 212.86.125[.]24, 213.111.148[.]90, 94.154.32[.]160. Novel Aura-targeting IPs from June 19-22: 103.75.11[.]78 and 103.75.11[.]110.
- MITRE coverage: T1566.004, T1528, T1671, T1213.004, T1567. All three paths avoided triggering traditional sign-in anomalies because actors operated through pre-approved apps and trusted identities.
Hunt: the KQL queries in the report pivot on CloudAppEvents for ApiTotalUsage, ReportExport, UniqueQuery, and SSO actions. Cross-reference against the published IOCs and flag connected apps inactive 90+ days.

item.description:

item.title: Threat Actors Achieve Persistence After SQL Injection
item.description:
SQL injection on an IIS/MSSQL host led to BadIIS module installation, XMRig deployment, and a new local admin account, all in a single June 2026 intrusion at a tech-sector org.
Key findings:
- Initial access via unsanitized user input on an IIS-hosted web page, giving the attacker execution through sqlservr.exe. Recon followed immediately: tasklist /svc output was exfiltrated via PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest POST to 334thribetlhkyo977gqrcht1k7bvdj2.oastify[.]com, a Burp Collaborator-style callback domain.
- Persistence was layered: Terminal Services re-enabled, a new local admin account named adminweb2$ created and used for RDP authentication, BadIIS modules HttpFastCgiModule.dll and HttpCgiModule.dll installed via appcmd.exe for SEO fraud and traffic redirection, and XMRig dropped as a resilient Windows service using nssm.exe.
- Miner files edge.exe and Taskgmr.ps1 were planted in C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\ with system, hidden, archive, and read-only attributes set via attrib.exe to blend in. CnCrypt Protect was added for further defense evasion. Windows Defender was disabled, but EDR was left untouched.
- Malicious scripts including qdcjoke1.2.ps1 and qd_tjoke.bat were staged in C:\Users\Public\ and C:\ProgramData\tjoke\, downloaded from pub-c4c8e8c336c3429d97195076bf3bb6eb.r2[.]dev.

item.title: Dark Web Profile: Krybit Ransomware
item.description:
Krybit Ransomware, a Babuk-derived RaaS active since late March 2026, gained unusual early visibility when a rival group breached its affiliate panel and exposed plaintext credentials, Bitcoin wallets, and victim data less than a month after launch.
- Krybit is built on Babuk's leaked 2021 source code (ESET: Filecoder.Babyk.A, Microsoft: Babuk!ic), not custom-engineered malware. It offers affiliates an 80/20 revenue split and builders for Windows, Linux, VMware ESXi, and NAS, making it a cross-platform threat from day one. Ransom demands run $40,000-$100,000 with 10-250GB of staged exfiltration per victim.
- The April 2026 breach by rival 0APT exposed the full affiliate panel: 2 operators (KRYBIT, GREP), 5 affiliates, 20 active victim negotiations, 5 Bitcoin wallets with zero confirmed payments, and credentials stored in plaintext with no hashing. Krybit retaliated by compromising 0APT's server and defacing its DLS. SOCRadar now tracks 70 attributed victims across 43 countries, with Professional Services (21.4%), Technology (17.1%), and Manufacturing (14.3%) as top sectors.
- Key forensic markers: encrypted files carry the .KRYBIT extension, ransom note is RECOVER-README.txt, and the group runs vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (T1490) before encryption. Initial access maps to T1078 and T1021.001 (RDP with compromised credentials). Five .onion DLS domains are confirmed, listed below defanged.

item.title: Australia Alerts Organizations to Ongoing CMS Exploitation Attacks
item.description:
Australia 🇦🇺's Signals Directorate warns of a global CMS exploitation campaign hitting WordPress, Joomla, and Craft CMS with 17 CVEs, deploying webshells for persistent access and lateral movement into corporate networks.
- Attackers are mass-scanning for 17 known, patched CVEs across WordPress plugins (Ninja Forms CVE-2026-0740, Gravity Forms CVE-2025-12352, WPvivid Backup CVE-2026-1357, Breeze Cache CVE-2026-3844, GutenKit likely CVE-2024-9234) plus Craft CMS CVE-2025-32432 and Joomla JCE CVE-2026-48907. Vuln classes are unauthenticated file upload, RCE, SSRF, and deserialization. Every successful hit is an unpatched system.
- The kill chain is scan, exploit, drop webshell, pivot. Once a webshell lands in a plugin or upload directory, actors use it for credential harvesting, malware staging, defacement, or as a jump point into internal corporate networks. That last pivot turns a neglected WordPress site into a corporate incident.
- The ACSC ties the campaign's pace to AI-accelerated exploit development, shrinking the window between public CVE disclosure and active exploitation. Five Eyes agencies flagged this trend jointly; this campaign is the live evidence.
- For IR: check web directories (especially plugin folders) for unexpected files. Hunt access logs for anomalous GET/POST requests to unknown paths. If a webshell is found, do not just delete it.

item.title: Someone Is Scanning for Your MCP Servers and AI Assistant Credentials, (Mon, Jul 13th)
item.description:
Internet-wide scanning is now probing for MCP servers, AI assistant credential files, and unauthenticated LLM endpoints. Observed on a low-traffic host with no AI infrastructure, confirming this is broad opportunistic recon, not targeted.
Key findings:
- POST /mcp requests carried valid JSON-RPC 2.0 MCP initialize handshakes from 49 distinct source IPs. These are not dumb URL probes; the scanner speaks the protocol and waits for a compliant response before enumerating exposed tools and data sources. An unauthenticated MCP server is a machine-readable inventory of everything an agent can touch.
- Credential file fishing targeted /.claude/.credentials.json, /.claude/mcp.json, /.cursor/mcp.json, and /.vscode/mcp.json using HEAD requests to check existence before downloading. AI assistant secrets now sit inside the same wordlists as AWS, GCP, Azure, and Kubernetes credential files.
- GET /v1/models (OpenAI-compatible) and GET /api/tags (Ollama) probe for unauthenticated local LLM endpoints. A hit means free compute for the attacker and a potential pivot.
- SSRF probes rotated across url, uri, path, and dest parameters targeting the GCP metadata endpoint. Agent tooling with fetch-style helpers is a natural SSRF primitive for this technique.
Hunt: grep access logs for POST /mcp, GET /sse, GET /v1/models, and GET /api/tags. Any hit on a host with no AI stack is pure recon.

item.title: Anatomy of a helpdesk social engineering attack (and how to stop MFA bypass)
item.description:
Scattered Spider and copycat actors are bypassing MFA entirely through helpdesk social engineering, not malware. AI-assisted voice cloning and PII scraping have made this attack chain nearly frictionless in 2026.
Key findings:
- Attack chain: recon via data brokers and LinkedIn builds a PII profile, then a caller impersonates the employee, defeats knowledge-based verification, and convinces helpdesk to reset the password and re-enroll MFA to an attacker-controlled device. No exploit, no malware, just a phone call.
- Once inside the cloud account, threat actors scrape emails for credentials, pivot to document shares, send fraudulent invoices to suppliers, or use residential proxies to blend sessions so the access looks entirely routine, including satisfied MFA on an enrolled device.
- If only a password reset is obtained, push bombing follows: flooding the real user with approval prompts until one is accepted, or calling helpdesk back to have the login manually approved.
- Detection still exists even after a clean social engineering call: MFA device enrollment events, impossible travel, new device sign-ins, and off-hours resets all surface in cloud telemetry. Correlate those signals rather than waiting for a single alert.
Treat MFA re-enrollment as a privileged action requiring manager approval or callback to a pre-enrolled number, never PII alone. Migrate toward FIDO2 or passkeys to eliminate push bombing and SIM-swap risk entirely.

item.title: GigaWiper Merges Three Malware Families Into One Destructive Backdoor
item.description:
GigaWiper merges three malware families into a single Go backdoor combining espionage, remote control, and on-demand disk destruction. Microsoft discovered it during active wiping activity in October 2025.
- Built in Go, GigaWiper communicates via RabbitMQ on port 5544 for command delivery and Redis on port 7542 for results, both pointing to C2 at 185.182.193[.]21. A RabbitMQ fanout exchange named "All" can blast destruction commands to every infected host simultaneously, while a "Topic" exchange enables targeted tasking.
- Persistence lives in a scheduled task named "OneDrive Update" firing every minute and at startup, with execution count tracked in a registry key disguised as a OneDrive entry. Command 19 wipes Windows event logs using two separate deletion methods if the first fails, directly targeting forensic visibility.
- The destructive command set covers raw disk overwrite (Command 1), BSOD plus boot file deletion (Command 2), fake ransomware with .candy extension and irrecoverable encryption (Command 3, derived from Crucio ransomware), and a multi-pass zero/0xFF/random wipe of the Windows drive (Command 12, a Go port of FlockWiper). No ransom note exists because recovery was never intended.

item.title: This new Windows malware can take over your PC and wipe it clean
item.description:
GigaWiper, a modular Golang backdoor for Windows, blends espionage, remote access, and multi-method data destruction in a single framework observed in intrusions since October 2025.
Key findings:
- Built from prior tools: GigaWiper wraps Crucio ransomware and FlockWiper disk wiper into one platform, implementing roughly 20 commands across three categories: destruction, remote access/monitoring, and system management. - Persistence via a scheduled task named "OneDrive Update" running every minute and at startup (T1053.005). Remote control runs over a TCP desktop-streaming server that self-carves Windows Firewall exceptions to stay reachable.
- C2 infrastructure: 185.182.193[.]21 and 212.8.248[.]104. Malwarebytes detects components as Trojan.FlockWiper and Backdoor.GigaWiper.

item.title: The AI Agent Credential Crisis: From Stealer Log to Source Code
item.description:
Stealer logs now target AI coding agents, turning a single infected developer machine into a key for source code, cloud infra, and CI/CD pipelines. Over 3.1 million OpenAI credentials were compromised in 2025 alone.
Key findings:
- SOCRadar analyzed stealer log data across 2025 and found 3.1M+ records tied to OpenAI, with total AI/developer platform exposure exceeding 3M accounts. Replit (204K) and Hugging Face (186K) followed, platforms where credentials carry write access to repos, datasets, and deployment pipelines. Three malware families, LummaC2 (56%), RedLine (17%), and StealC (13%), account for 86% of all observed logs.
- The multiplier effect is the core risk. A stolen AI agent credential is not one account. It bundles OAuth tokens for GitHub/GitLab orgs, AWS/GCP/Azure keys, CI/CD pipeline tokens, package registry creds, and MCP integrations for Slack, Jira, and Sentry into a single harvested session. Infostealers harvest .env files, .claude/settings.json, and browser-synced session cookies without distinguishing personal from corporate devices.
- The quarterly curve tells a disruption story. Q1 peaked at 953K records, then a May 2025 law enforcement action against LummaC2 C2 infrastructure drove a 42% volume drop through Q3 (553K). By Q4, volumes recovered to 857K as operators rebuilt and newer families like Acreed and MacSync filled the gap. Temporary wins, not structural defeat.

item.title: Dell BIOS Passwords: Weak XOR Encryption Allows Recovery from SPI Flash (CVE-2026-40639)
item.description:
CVE-2026-40639: Dell BIOS passwords stored under reversible XOR encryption in SPI flash, recoverable in milliseconds with a chip programmer. Actively unpatched on the Wyse 5070 thin client as of today.
Key findings:
- Dell's SystemPwSmm SMM driver stores BIOS admin/user passwords as XOR-encrypted data in the DVAR region of SPI flash, not a hash. The first byte is stored in cleartext. For passwords up to 12 characters, null-padding in the 32-byte field leaks the entire 20-byte key directly. No brute force needed.
- The key is derived from mostly device-static data plus the cleartext first byte, meaning only 256 possible keys exist per device. DVAR is log-structured, so deleted password records persist on flash. A short historical password with the same first character hands you the key to decrypt a longer current one.
- Confirmed vulnerable: Latitude E7250, Latitude 7490, XPS 15 9560, Wyse 5070. Not vulnerable: OptiPlex 3000 and newer models using SIVB with SHA-256. DSA-2026-197 patches Edge Gateway and Precision lines; the Wyse 5070 and confirmed-vulnerable Latitudes are not in that first wave. Dell targets remaining fixes by end of July 2026.
- CVSS 3.1 scored 5.7 by Dell (AV:P/AC:H), 6.1 by researchers (AV:P/AC:L). Physical access to flash is required via SOIC clip or attacker-controlled OS boot. Impact: disables Secure Boot, changes boot order, and can break TPM-backed BitLocker chains if unmeasured settings are modified.

item.title: Conditional Access Misconfigurations Exposed 55 Orgs with MFA On
item.description:
Two separate M365 campaigns bypassed MFA across 64+ orgs by exploiting Conditional Access blind spots: device code phishing via Railway PaaS and ROPC credential spray via LSHIY LLC's IPv6 range.
Key findings:
- Railway campaign (March 2026): EvilTokens PhaaS weaponized OAuth device code flow (T1528), harvesting tokens from legitimate Microsoft endpoints. Railway's clean IP reputation defeated Identity Protection risk scoring. Three Railway IPs drove ~84% of attack traffic across 344 orgs in the US 🇺🇸, Canada 🇨🇦, Australia 🇦🇺, New Zealand 🇳🇿, and Germany 🇩🇪. Tokens persist up to 90 days, surviving password resets.
- LSHIY campaign: 81 million ROPC requests hit the /token endpoint directly, bypassing the authorization endpoint entirely. MFA Conditional Access never fired because Azure CLI was excluded. 55 of 78 compromised accounts had active MFA policies, yet were still breached.
- CA policy failures observed: MFA scoped to specific apps not "All Cloud Apps," group-scoped policies missing compromised accounts, trusted location mislabeled as US-based, and one tenant with a policy explicitly named "Block Azure CLI" that did not block Azure CLI.
- Detection opportunity: hunt Azure AD sign-in logs for successful authentications where clientAppUsed equals "Device Code" or "ROPC" and cross-reference against accounts not in legacy auth exception groups.
Audit your CA policies against All Cloud Apps, All Users, All Client App Types.

item.title: Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)
item.description:
AI coding agents across six major platforms can be tricked into writing attacker SSH keys or shell configs via symlink-poisoned repos, no memory corruption required. The GhostApproval research from Wiz exposes a decades-old primitive wearing a new disguise.
Key details:
- The attack chain stacks three failures: prompt injection via README instructions aimed at the agent, symlink traversal without path resolution, and a confirmation dialog that shows the friendly filename (project_settings.json) while hiding the real target (~/.ssh/authorized_keys or ~/.zshrc). Remove any one link and the attack fizzles. Git stores symlinks with file mode 120000, blob content is the raw target path, and recreates them faithfully on clone on Linux and macOS.
- Six agents tested: Amazon Q Developer, Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf. All showed variations of the flaw. In several, the write completed before a confirmation dialog appeared. In the Claude Code case, the agent's own internal reasoning correctly identified the real target file, then the dialog told the human it was editing "project_settings.json." CWE-61 covers the symlink following; CWE-451 covers the UI misrepresentation. AWS, Google, and Cursor shipped fixes.
- Prior art matters for scoping: CVE-2024-32002 abused symlinks plus submodules to drop into .git/hooks and execute code on git clone --recurse-submodules.

item.title: Not-so-anonymous telemetry: The @injectivelabs/sdk-ts backdoor
item.description:
Supply chain attack hit @injectivelabs/sdk-ts v1.20.21, stealing BIP-39 seed phrases and raw private keys from a finance-focused blockchain SDK with ~175,000 monthly downloads. Window of exposure: 49 minutes.
- Malicious commit 0121928 was pushed July 8 at 8:24 p.m. UTC directly to the main branch, appearing to originate from a legitimate maintainer's account. Git metadata showed the commits came from a UTC-4 timezone machine never previously used by that committer, a forensic signal suggesting account compromise or session hijacking rather than a rogue insider.
- The attack hooked PrivateKey.fromMnemonic() and PrivateKey.fromHex() inside packages/sdk-ts/src/core/accounts/PrivateKey.ts. Every time a wallet loaded, the full 12/24-word seed phrase or raw private key string was passed to trackKeyDerivation(), base64-encoded, and smuggled in the X-Request-Id HTTP header to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective[.]network, a domain crafted to blend with legitimate Injective gRPC infrastructure. The exfil endpoint was still live at time of writing.
- Deception was layered: the new file carried a convincing docblock describing anonymous SDK telemetry and timing metrics, and the C2 domain was built at runtime from a character-code array to resist static analysis.
- Only @injectivelabs/sdk-ts version 1.20.21 is confirmed malicious. Versions before 1.20.21 and 1.20.23 onward are clean.

item.title: The Two BIOS Passwords Everyone Confuses
item.description:
"We set the BIOS password" is not a complete sentence. Setup password and boot password protect different things, and mixing them up leaves firmware-level gaps on every machine in the fleet.
Key findings:
- The setup (administrator) password gates firmware config changes: Secure Boot state, boot order, TPM, IOMMU. It does NOT prompt at power-on. A stolen laptop with only this set boots straight to the OS. The boot (power-on) password is what stops the machine from starting at all. One password does not cover the other.
- Vendor naming makes this worse. Lenovo calls them Supervisor + Power-On, Dell calls them Admin + System, HP calls them BIOS Administrator + Power-On. A policy or ticket that says "set the BIOS password" has not actually specified which control was configured.
- Setting the admin password does not automatically lock configuration changes. There is a separate setting to prevent boot-order and Secure Boot edits when an admin password is present. Miss it and the password is half the control it should be.
- Eclypsium's flash-dump research found at least one vendor storing the admin password in plaintext ASCII in a firmware variable, and another using a short, truncated hash built from a static key, making it crackable offline and identical across every unit of that model.
Audit state, not policy. Read the actual password-set flag per device via /sys/class/firmware-attributes/ on Linux or vendor WMI namespaces on Windows.

item.title: Finding SOCKS with Proxywatch
item.description:
SpecterOps releases Proxywatch, a behavior-based open-source tool to detect SOCKS proxy pivots, C2 beaconing, and tunneling activity on live endpoints without relying on static signatures or process-port baselines.
- SOCKS proxy pivoting lets attackers run tools like Impacket, nmap, or netexec entirely from their own machine through a compromised host, meaning no new processes spawn on the victim, no attacker tooling touches disk, and EDR parent-child detection models see nothing. C2 frameworks like Cobalt Strike, Sliver, and Mythic all support this natively. This is why registry persistence created via Impacket reg.py over SOCKS gets missed: the code never executes on-target.
- Proxywatch runs on Linux and Windows, reading /proc/net/tcp and /proc/<pid>/fd on Linux, and GetExtendedTcpTable plus CreateToolhelp32Snapshot on Windows. It builds per-process behavioral profiles using 83 signals including loopback usage, multiplex relay patterns, callback cadence, jitter measurement, writable-path binaries, and named pipe C2 patterns, then assigns roles: control-channel, control-pivot, listener, or outbound.
- In a live demo, cheerful_glove.exe (a Sliver beacon) was flagged control-pivot via signals pivot-multiplex-relay and pivot-non-loopback-internal. A separate beacon, beacon-j.exe, was caught via a 75-second callback pattern with 0.44 jitter, unsigned binary, and suspicious-exe-path (C:\Users\ops\Desktop\testing\).

item.title: GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware
item.description:
GigaWiper is a Golang backdoor that merges three separate destructive malware families into a single modular implant, observed wiping targets since October 2025.
- GigaWiper combines a raw disk wiper, a Crucio ransomware-derived fake encryptor (command 3, .candy extension, keys never saved), and a reimplemented FlockWiper secure multi-pass wiper (command 12) as discrete C2 commands. C2 runs over RabbitMQ (AMQP) and Redis with AES-encrypted config; observed C2 IPs are 185.182.193[.]21 and 212.8.248[.]104.
- Persistence lands via a scheduled task named "OneDrive Update" (runs every minute plus at startup) and tracks execution count in HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment. Command 19 clears System, Setup, Application, and Security event logs, including a direct delete of C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Security.evtx if wevtutil fails.
- Code overlap links GigaWiper to Crucio (CISA advisory, Dec 2023) via shared BigBangExtortMain function, and to FlockWiper (VirusTotal, June 2025) via PDB paths referencing "GRAT" and identical execution flow, suggesting one actor built all three tools.
- IOC hashes (4 backdoor, 1 standalone wiper, 1 Crucio, 2 FlockWiper) and both C2 IPs are in the Microsoft report. Microsoft Defender detections include WprFlock, WprCree, FlockWiper, and GigaWiper signatures.

item.title: Hiding in the Chain: Multi-Stage LNK Attack Leveraging TON Blockchain to Deliver Node.JS Backdoor
item.description:
Multi-stage LNK attack uses TON blockchain as a C2 resolver and drops a Node.js backdoor, making traditional domain-based blocking ineffective against this campaign.
Key findings:
- Initial access via a malicious ZIP containing a .lnk file. When executed, the shortcut fires a hidden PowerShell command (T1059.001) that downloads a legitimate node.exe binary and deploys a Node.js backdoor, blending malicious traffic with a trusted runtime.
- The malware uses EtherHiding (T1102): querying the TON blockchain to retrieve the live C2 address. Blocking a domain or IP does nothing here because the C2 pointer lives on an immutable ledger, not a registrar-controlled hostname.

item.title: Januscape: 16-Year-Old Linux KVM Bug Enables Cloud VM Escape Attacks
item.description:
CVE-2026-53359 "Januscape": a 16-year-old use-after-free in Linux KVM's shadow MMU lets a guest VM crash or potentially escape to the host, affecting both Intel and AMD x86 clouds exposing nested virtualization.
- CVE-2026-53359 lives in kvm_mmu_get_child_sp(), where KVM matched shadow page candidates by memory address alone, ignoring the page role type. A guest with root can race the shadow MMU until host kernel memory is corrupted. The public PoC reliably panics the host, taking every co-tenant VM down with it. A full code-execution exploit exists but has not been released.
- Attack prerequisites: root inside the guest (standard on any rented cloud VM) plus nested virtualization exposed by the host. The bug sits in in-kernel KVM, not QEMU, so custom cloud stacks that strip QEMU are not protected. GCP and AWS instances with nested virt enabled are the primary threat surface.
- On RHEL-family hosts where /dev/kvm is world-writable (0666), an unprivileged local user can trigger the bug without a VM at all, achieving host privilege escalation directly.

item.title: Chaining a DOM XSS Sink, WAF Bypass, Cross-Origin Smuggling, and SDK Abuse into One Click Account…
item.description:
A four-bug chain, DOM XSS sink, Akamai WAF bypass via window.name smuggling, and SDK abuse, delivered a one-click account takeover including live AWS STS credentials from two separate AWS accounts.
- The sink: an error-page React component reads a backURL query parameter and passes it to window.location.assign with zero scheme validation. Any javascript: URI executes in the target origin. The only gate is that the button label must read "Reload Page" or "Please try again," both reachable via legitimate error paths.
- The WAF bypass: after 80+ probes, the pattern emerged. Akamai's rule blocks keyword-paren adjacency (alert(, eval(, Function(). Property-access syntax breaks that adjacency. The payload javascript:top["setTimeout"](name) passes HTTP 200 because no keyword sits directly next to a paren.
- The smuggling: window.name persists across cross-origin navigations and is not governed by SOP. The attacker sets window.name to the full payload on their own page, then redirects the victim. Akamai never sees the payload, only a clean dispatcher URL. setTimeout evaluates window.name as code inside the target origin.
- The SDK escalation: every page loaded a global auth SDK exposing getJWTToken() and getTempAWSCreds(). HttpOnly cookies were irrelevant; the SDK made credentialed XHR calls and returned signed JWTs and live AWS STS credentials directly to the executing script, two AWS accounts, in under 10 seconds.

item.title: The HTTP 303 SSRF Hack : From Python HTTP Client Defaults to AWS Credential Exfiltration.
item.description:
A blind SSRF escalated to live AWS IAM credential theft by chaining a user-controlled OAuth field, Python requests default redirect handling, and IMDSv1 reachability on an EKS node. No single component was broken. The composition was.
- BigQuery service account JSON accepted by the platform contained a user-supplied token_uri field with zero allowlist validation. The backend passed it verbatim to the google-auth library, which POSTed a signed JWT to whatever URL the attacker provided. An OOB Interactsh probe confirmed the primitive immediately.
- Direct SSRF to 169.254.169[.]254 failed because IMDS returns HTTP 405 to POST requests. Timing analysis (IMDS responded in 0.34s vs. 28s for an unroutable IP) proved the pod could reach IMDS, the verb was simply wrong. The fix: serve HTTP 303 See Other from an attacker-controlled server. Per RFC 7231 §6.4.4, Python requests rewrites POST to GET on a 303, strips the body, and follows the Location header to IMDS.
- The error reflection channel completed the read primitive. google-auth parsed the IMDS JSON response, failed to find access_token, raised an exception, and the worker returned the raw exception string, including AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken, in the HTTP 400 body to the authenticated caller.
- Remediation: the platform implemented a frozenset allowlist at the field-parsing layer, blocking any token_uri not matching oauth2.googleapis[.]com/token or accounts.google[.]com/o/oauth2/token.

item.title: CVE-2026-48282: Adobe ColdFusion RDS Path Traversal Leading to RCE
item.description:

The handler passed user-supplied paths directly to the file system without canonicalization, letting traversal sequences like ..\ or absolute paths escape the RDS root and write anywhere the ColdFusion service account can reach, including the web root.

item.title: The File That Answered Back — XXE Hidden in Cell A2
item.description:
Unauthenticated XXE via XLSX upload bypasses WAF and reads arbitrary server files. A crafted spreadsheet delivered three confirmed in-band file reads against a production endpoint with no authentication required.
Key findings:
- The target endpoint, /[REDACTED]/personal/CombineExcelUpload, processed Excel uploads server-side and reflected cell values directly in JSON responses. No session token or authentication was required. The WAF (Imperva) was absent on this Alibaba Cloud host behind an F5 load balancer, so the DOCTYPE keyword that was blocked elsewhere passed through untouched.
- Attack chain: a hand-built XLSX (a ZIP of five XML files) had the XXE payload injected into xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml. The DOCTYPE entity declaration pointed to file:///C:/windows/win.ini. The .NET XML parser resolved the entity, substituted file contents into cell A2, and the app returned them in the uploadResult JSON field. Three reads confirmed: win.ini, system32/drivers/etc/hosts, and system.ini.
- Root cause is .NET's insecure XML parser default. XmlReaderSettings with DtdProcessing left at its default allows external entity resolution. The fix is two lines: DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit and XmlResolver = null, or switching to EPPlus or ClosedXML which disable XXE by design.
- Further escalation was blocked: web.config contains XML markup that breaks inline substitution, and outbound DTD callbacks for CDATA-wrapping were blocked at the load balancer.
